Problem 2.2.1 Easy Google

QUESTION: Given a small 1D dataset of $N=3$ observations: $$(x_1, y_1) = (1, 2), \quad (x_2, y_2) = (2, 3), \quad (x_3, y_3) = (3, 5)$$

  1. Construct the augmented feature matrix $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 2}$ and target vector $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 1}$.
  2. Compute the Gram matrix $\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}$, its determinant, and its inverse $(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1}$ by hand.
  3. Compute the OLS solution vector $\mathbf{w}^* = [b^*, w_1^*]^T$ and calculate the predicted values $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ and residuals $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}$.
✓ Complete Step-by-Step Numerical Solution

Step 1: Construct Augmented Matrices: $$\mathbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}$$

Step 2: Compute $\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}$ and Its Inverse: $$\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1+1+1 & 1+2+3 \\ 1+2+3 & 1+4+9 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ 6 & 14 \end{bmatrix}$$ Determinant: $$\det(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}) = (3)(14) - (6)(6) = 42 - 36 = 6$$ Matrix inverse using formula for $2 \times 2$ matrices $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad-bc} \begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}$: $$(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} = \frac{1}{6} \begin{bmatrix} 14 & -6 \\ -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7/3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1/2 \end{bmatrix}$$

Step 3: Compute $\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}$ and Parameter Vector $\mathbf{w}^*$: $$\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2+3+5 \\ 2+6+15 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 23 \end{bmatrix}$$ Multiply by inverse: $$\mathbf{w}^* = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y} = \frac{1}{6} \begin{bmatrix} 14 & -6 \\ -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 23 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{6} \begin{bmatrix} 140 - 138 \\ -60 + 69 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{6} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1/3 \\ 3/2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.3333 \\ 1.5000 \end{bmatrix}$$ Model equation: $\hat{y} = 1.5 x + 0.3333$.

Step 4: Predictions and Residuals: $$\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}^* = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1/3 \\ 3/2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1/3 + 3/2 \\ 1/3 + 3 \\ 1/3 + 9/2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 11/6 \\ 20/6 \\ 29/6 \end{bmatrix} \approx \begin{bmatrix} 1.8333 \\ 3.3333 \\ 4.8333 \end{bmatrix}$$ Residual vector $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}$: $$\mathbf{e} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 11/6 \\ 20/6 \\ 29/6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1/6 \\ -2/6 \\ 1/6 \end{bmatrix}$$ Check orthogonality $\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{e}$: $$\sum e_i = \frac{1}{6} - \frac{2}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = 0 \quad \checkmark$$ $$\sum x_i e_i = 1\left(\frac{1}{6}\right) + 2\left(-\frac{2}{6}\right) + 3\left(\frac{1}{6}\right) = \frac{1 - 4 + 3}{6} = 0 \quad \checkmark$$ Result: $\mathbf{w}^* = [1/3, 3/2]^T$, and residuals sum to exactly zero, confirming OLS optimality.

Problem 2.2.2 Easy Meta

QUESTION: Using the same data from Problem 2.2.1, compute the Ridge Regression solution with regularization penalty parameter $\lambda = 2.0$ (penalizing only the slope $w_1$, keeping intercept $b$ unpenalized).

✓ Complete Step-by-Step Numerical Solution

Step 1: Construct the Regularized Matrix:
We penalize $w_1$ by adding $\lambda = 2.0$ to the $(2, 2)$ position of $\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}$: $$\mathbf{A}_{\text{Ridge}} = \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ 6 & 14 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 \\ 6 & 16 \end{bmatrix}$$

Step 2: Invert $\mathbf{A}_{\text{Ridge}}$: $$\det(\mathbf{A}_{\text{Ridge}}) = (3)(16) - (6)(6) = 48 - 36 = 12$$ $$\mathbf{A}_{\text{Ridge}}^{-1} = \frac{1}{12} \begin{bmatrix} 16 & -6 \\ -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$

Step 3: Solve for $\mathbf{w}^*_{\text{Ridge}}$: $$\mathbf{w}^*_{\text{Ridge}} = \frac{1}{12} \begin{bmatrix} 16 & -6 \\ -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 23 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{12} \begin{bmatrix} 160 - 138 \\ -60 + 69 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{12} \begin{bmatrix} 22 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 11/6 \\ 3/4 \end{bmatrix} \approx \begin{bmatrix} 1.8333 \\ 0.7500 \end{bmatrix}$$ Comparison with OLS: $$\text{OLS Slope: } w_1^* = 1.5000 \quad \longrightarrow \quad \text{Ridge Slope: } w_{1,\text{Ridge}}^* = 0.7500$$ Result: Ridge regularization shrunk the slope by exactly $50\%$, dampening model sensitivity to noise!

Tier 2: Applied Engineering & Algorithmic Tracing

Problem 2.2.3 Medium Apple

QUESTION: In coordinate descent for Lasso regression, the soft-thresholding operator is defined as: $$S_\lambda(\rho) = \text{sign}(\rho) \max(|\rho| - \lambda, 0)$$ Assume centered and normalized features ($\mathbf{x}_j^T \mathbf{x}_j = 1$). For a 2-variable problem with target $\mathbf{y}$, let $\lambda = 1.5$. Trace one full cycle of Coordinate Descent across variables $w_1$ and $w_2$, starting from initial weights $(w_1^{(0)}, w_2^{(0)}) = (0.0, 0.0)$, given: $$\mathbf{x}_1^T \mathbf{y} = 3.0, \quad \mathbf{x}_2^T \mathbf{y} = 1.2, \quad \mathbf{x}_1^T \mathbf{x}_2 = 0.5$$

✓ Complete Step-by-Step Algorithmic Trace

Step 1: Update $w_1$ while fixing $w_2 = 0$:
Partial residual correlation for feature 1: $$\rho_1 = \mathbf{x}_1^T (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}_2 w_2^{(0)}) = \mathbf{x}_1^T \mathbf{y} - (\mathbf{x}_1^T \mathbf{x}_2)(0) = 3.0 - 0 = 3.0$$ Apply soft-thresholding with $\lambda = 1.5$: $$|\rho_1| = 3.0 > 1.5 \implies w_1^{(1)} = \text{sign}(3.0) \times (3.0 - 1.5) = \mathbf{+1.50}$$

Step 2: Update $w_2$ using updated $w_1 = 1.50$:
Partial residual correlation for feature 2: $$\rho_2 = \mathbf{x}_2^T (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}_1 w_1^{(1)}) = \mathbf{x}_2^T \mathbf{y} - (\mathbf{x}_1^T \mathbf{x}_2) w_1^{(1)}$$ $$\rho_2 = 1.2 - (0.5)(1.50) = 1.2 - 0.75 = \mathbf{0.45}$$ Apply soft-thresholding with $\lambda = 1.5$: $$|\rho_2| = 0.45 \le \lambda = 1.5$$ Since $|\rho_2| \le \lambda$, the soft-thresholding operator zeros out the coefficient: $$w_2^{(1)} = S_{1.5}(0.45) = \mathbf{0.0}$$ Result after Cycle 1: $\mathbf{w}^{(1)} = [1.50, 0.0]^T$. Feature 2 is set to exact zero, demonstrating Lasso's automatic sparse feature selection.

Problem 2.2.4 Medium Amazon

QUESTION: For the dataset in Problem 2.2.1 ($\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 2}$):

  1. Explicitly compute all 9 entries of the $3 \times 3$ Hat Matrix $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T$.
  2. Verify that the trace of $\mathbf{H}$ equals the number of parameters ($p = 2$).
  3. Verify that $\mathbf{H}^2 = \mathbf{H}$ (Idempotence) by calculating $\mathbf{H} \mathbf{H}$.
✓ Complete Step-by-Step Matrix Solution

Step 1: Compute Hat Matrix $\mathbf{H}$:
From Problem 2.2.1: $$(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} = \frac{1}{6} \begin{bmatrix} 14 & -6 \\ -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ First compute $\mathbf{X} (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1}$: $$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \frac{1}{6} \begin{bmatrix} 14 & -6 \\ -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{6} \begin{bmatrix} 14-6 & -6+3 \\ 14-12 & -6+6 \\ 14-18 & -6+9 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{6} \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -3 \\ 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$ Now multiply by $\mathbf{X}^T = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$: $$\mathbf{H} = \frac{1}{6} \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -3 \\ 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{6} \begin{bmatrix} 8-3 & 8-6 & 8-9 \\ 2+0 & 2+0 & 2+0 \\ -4+3 & -4+6 & -4+9 \end{bmatrix}$$ $$\mathbf{H} = \frac{1}{6} \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$$

Step 2: Check Trace: $$\text{Tr}(\mathbf{H}) = \frac{5 + 2 + 5}{6} = \frac{12}{6} = \mathbf{2}$$ This matches the number of parameters $d+1 = 2$ ($b$ and $w_1$).

Step 3: Check Idempotence ($\mathbf{H}^2 = \mathbf{H}$): $$\mathbf{H}^2 = \frac{1}{36} \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ Row 1, Col 1: $(25 + 4 + 1) = 30 = 6 \times 5$. Divided by 36: $5/6$.
Row 1, Col 2: $(10 + 4 - 2) = 12 = 6 \times 2$. Divided by 36: $2/6$.
Row 1, Col 3: $(-5 + 4 - 5) = -6 = 6 \times (-1)$. Divided by 36: $-1/6$.
Evaluating all entries identically returns $\frac{1}{6} \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 5 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{H}$.
Q.E.D. The Hat matrix is symmetric and idempotent with trace equal to parameter dimension!

Tier 3: FAANG & Research Lab Challenges

Problem 2.2.5 Hard Google DeepMind Meta

QUESTION: Prove the Gauss-Markov Theorem for linear regression from first principles. Specifically, let $\hat{\mathbf{w}} = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}$ be the OLS estimator. Let $\tilde{\mathbf{w}} = \mathbf{C} \mathbf{y}$ be any other arbitrary linear unbiased estimator of $\mathbf{w}^*$. Prove that the difference between their covariance matrices:

$$\text{Cov}(\tilde{\mathbf{w}}) - \text{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf{w}})$$

is a Positive Semi-Definite (PSD) matrix, proving that OLS achieves minimum variance in every linear projection direction $\mathbf{a}^T \text{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf{w}}) \mathbf{a} \le \mathbf{a}^T \text{Cov}(\tilde{\mathbf{w}}) \mathbf{a}$.

✓ Complete Step-by-Step Mathematical Proof

Step 1: Characterize the Linear Estimator:
Let $\tilde{\mathbf{w}} = \mathbf{C} \mathbf{y}$ where $\mathbf{C} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times N}$.
Define the deviation from the OLS matrix: $\mathbf{D} = \mathbf{C} - (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T$.
Thus, $\mathbf{C} = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T + \mathbf{D}$.

Step 2: Enforce the Unbiasedness Constraint:
For $\tilde{\mathbf{w}}$ to be an unbiased estimator of $\mathbf{w}^*$: $$\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathbf{w}}] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{C}\mathbf{y}] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}^* + \boldsymbol{\epsilon})] = \mathbf{C}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}^* + \mathbf{C}\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}] = \mathbf{C}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}^*$$ For $\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathbf{w}}] = \mathbf{w}^*$ to hold for all possible vectors $\mathbf{w}^*$, we must have: $$\mathbf{C} \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{I}_d$$ Substitute $\mathbf{C} = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T + \mathbf{D}$: $$((\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T + \mathbf{D}) \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{I}_d \implies (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}) + \mathbf{D} \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{I}_d \implies \mathbf{I}_d + \mathbf{D} \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{I}_d$$ Therefore, unbiasedness strictly requires: $$\mathbf{D} \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{0}$$

Step 3: Compute Covariance Matrix of $\tilde{\mathbf{w}}$:
Since $\tilde{\mathbf{w}} = \mathbf{C}\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}^* + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}) = \mathbf{w}^* + \mathbf{C}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$: $$\text{Cov}(\tilde{\mathbf{w}}) = \mathbb{E}[(\tilde{\mathbf{w}} - \mathbf{w}^*)(\tilde{\mathbf{w}} - \mathbf{w}^*)^T] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^T \mathbf{C}^T] = \mathbf{C} \mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^T] \mathbf{C}^T$$ By the homoscedasticity assumption $\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^T] = \sigma^2 \mathbf{I}_N$: $$\text{Cov}(\tilde{\mathbf{w}}) = \sigma^2 \mathbf{C} \mathbf{C}^T$$ Substitute $\mathbf{C} = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T + \mathbf{D}$: $$\mathbf{C} \mathbf{C}^T = \left( (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T + \mathbf{D} \right) \left( \mathbf{X} (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} + \mathbf{D}^T \right)$$ Expand the four terms: $$\mathbf{C} \mathbf{C}^T = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} + (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{D}^T + \mathbf{D} \mathbf{X} (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} + \mathbf{D} \mathbf{D}^T$$ Using $\mathbf{D} \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{0}$ and its transpose $\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{D}^T = \mathbf{0}^T = \mathbf{0}$: The middle two cross-terms vanish completely: $$\mathbf{C} \mathbf{C}^T = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} + \mathbf{D} \mathbf{D}^T$$

Step 4: Subtract the Covariances:
Recall that the OLS covariance is $\text{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf{w}}) = \sigma^2 (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1}$. Therefore: $$\text{Cov}(\tilde{\mathbf{w}}) - \text{Cov}(\hat{\mathbf{w}}) = \sigma^2 \left[ (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} + \mathbf{D}\mathbf{D}^T \right] - \sigma^2 (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} = \mathbf{\sigma^2 \mathbf{D} \mathbf{D}^T}$$ For any non-zero vector $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^d$: $$\mathbf{a}^T (\sigma^2 \mathbf{D} \mathbf{D}^T) \mathbf{a} = \sigma^2 (\mathbf{D}^T \mathbf{a})^T (\mathbf{D}^T \mathbf{a}) = \sigma^2 \|\mathbf{D}^T \mathbf{a}\|_2^2 \ge 0$$ The difference is strictly Positive Semi-Definite, achieving equality if and only if $\mathbf{D} = \mathbf{0}$ ($\tilde{\mathbf{w}} = \hat{\mathbf{w}}$).
Q.E.D. OLS is uniquely the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE)!

Problem 2.2.6 Hard OpenAI Anthropic

QUESTION: Prove mathematically why $L_1$ Lasso regularization induces exact sparsity ($w_j = 0$), whereas $L_2$ Ridge regularization only causes coefficient shrinkage ($w_j \to 0$ but $w_j \neq 0$). Use both the sub-gradient optimality conditions and the geometry of contour intersections.

✓ Complete Step-by-Step Mathematical Analysis

Step 1: Subdifferential Optimality of Lasso:
Consider a scalar objective with squared loss and regularizer: $$\mathcal{L}(w) = \frac{1}{2} (y - w)^2 + \lambda |w|$$ For $w \neq 0$, the derivative is $(w - y) + \lambda \text{sign}(w)$. Setting to zero: $$w = y - \lambda \text{ if } y > \lambda, \qquad w = y + \lambda \text{ if } y < -\lambda$$ At the point $w = 0$, the function $|w|$ is non-differentiable; its subdifferential is the set of all supporting slopes $\partial |w| = [-1, 1]$.
Fermat's optimality rule for non-smooth convex optimization states that $0$ is a global minimum if and only if $0 \in \partial \mathcal{L}(0)$: $$\partial \mathcal{L}(0) = (0 - y) + \lambda [-1, 1] = -y + [-\lambda, \lambda] = [-y - \lambda, \ -y + \lambda]$$ The condition $0 \in [-y - \lambda, -y + \lambda]$ holds whenever: $$-\lambda \le y \le \lambda \iff |y| \le \lambda$$ Key Insight: There is an entire continuous interval of empirical observations $[-\lambda, \lambda]$ of non-zero width $2\lambda$ where the exact optimal solution is locked onto $w^* = 0$!

Step 2: Contrast with Ridge $L_2$:
For Ridge: $$\mathcal{L}(w) = \frac{1}{2} (y - w)^2 + \frac{\lambda}{2} w^2 \implies \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w} = (w - y) + \lambda w = 0 \implies w^* = \frac{y}{1 + \lambda}$$ For any non-zero observation $y \neq 0$, $w^* = \frac{y}{1 + \lambda} \neq 0$. The Ridge estimate is zero if and only if the empirical observation $y$ is already identically zero (a set of measure zero).

Step 3: Geometric Intersection of Contours:
In constrained optimization, minimizing RSS subject to $\|\mathbf{w}\|_p \le C$ finds the point where the elliptical level curves of the RSS loss first touch the constraint ball:

  • The $L_1$ ball ($\sum |w_i| \le C$): A cross-polytope (rhombus in 2D) with sharp corners located precisely on the coordinate axes where other coordinates are zero ($w_1 = C, w_2 = 0$). Because the corners are non-smooth, the outward normal cone at the corners spans a wide angle ($90^\circ$). The expanding RSS ellipse has a massive probability of making its first contact at a corner point, forcing coordinates to exact zero.
  • The $L_2$ ball ($\sum w_i^2 \le C^2$): A smooth Euclidean sphere. The normal vector exists uniquely everywhere, so the ellipse touches the sphere at an arbitrary smooth point off the axes, keeping all weights non-zero.

Tier 4: Conceptual Trap MCQs & Assertion-Reasoning

Problem 2.2.7 Medium Google

QUESTION: In regularized linear regression (Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet), why do machine learning practitioners never regularize the bias term $b$ (intercept)?

  1. Regularizing the bias term causes the Hessian matrix to become singular.
  2. Regularizing the bias would make the model's predictions sensitive to shifting the origin of the target variable $y \to y + c$, causing systematic under-prediction of non-zero-centered targets.
  3. The derivative of the bias penalty cannot be computed in closed form.
  4. The bias term does not contribute to the variance of the model.
✓ Complete Conceptual Analysis & Explanation

Correct Option: B

Exhaustive Analysis of All Options:

  • Option B is TRUE: The intercept $b$ captures the global baseline average of the target $\bar{y}$. If the target is house prices centered around $\$500,000$, penalizing $b^2$ would shrink the predicted baseline toward $\$0$, introducing massive arbitrary bias simply because the target was not zero-centered. Regularization should constrain the model's sensitivity to feature variations (the slopes $w_j$), never the baseline location of the target distribution.
  • Option A is FALSE: Adding regularization to any parameter increases the diagonal of the Hessian, making it strictly more positive definite, not singular.
  • Option C is FALSE: The derivative of $\frac{\lambda}{2} b^2$ is simply $\lambda b$, trivially easy to compute.
  • Option D is FALSE: Estimating the bias from finite samples introduces variance $\sigma^2 / N$, but this is minimal and necessary to maintain an unbiased baseline.

Problem 2.2.8 Hard Microsoft

QUESTION: Consider the following Assertion (A) and Reason (R):

Assertion (A): Severe multicollinearity between features in a dataset inflates the variance of individual OLS regression weights $\text{Var}(\hat{w}_j) \to \infty$, but has virtually zero impact on the model's overall prediction accuracy on new test points that follow the exact same collinear covariance structure.

Reason (R): Multicollinearity means the feature matrix $\mathbf{X}$ has near-zero singular values along certain directions, causing the projection matrix $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T$ to become non-orthogonal.

  1. Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
  2. Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
  3. (A) is true, but (R) is false.
  4. (A) is false, but (R) is true.
✓ Complete Conceptual Analysis & Explanation

Correct Option: C

Exhaustive Analysis of Assertion & Reason:

  • Assertion (A) is TRUE: The Variance Inflation Factor is $\text{VIF}_j = \frac{1}{1 - R_j^2}$. As correlation approaches $1$, $\text{VIF} \to \infty$, and the algorithm cannot distinguish the separate effects of $w_1$ and $w_2$ (e.g. $w_1 + w_2 = 10$ could be fit as $1000$ and $-990$). However, for any test point where the two features maintain that same correlation, the sum $w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2$ remains stable and accurately predicts $y$.
  • Reason (R) is FALSE: The Hat matrix $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^T$ is always an orthogonal projection matrix ($\mathbf{H}^T = \mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{H}^2 = \mathbf{H}$) regardless of whether the features are collinear, as long as $(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})$ is invertible. Collinearity affects the orientation of the parameter space, not the mathematical orthogonality of the subspace projection.
  • Therefore, Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

5. Production Code Lab 2.2: OLS vs. Mini-Batch SGD from Scratch

Below is a production Python implementation comparing the exact analytical OLS Normal Equation against iterative Mini-Batch SGD with condition number tracking.

Code Lab 2.2 — OLS Normal Equations vs. Mini-Batch SGD

🔗 View in GitHub: part2_classical_ml/ch22_linear_regression/linear_regression_scratch.py

import numpy as np

class LinearRegressionScratch:
    def __init__(self, lr=0.01, batch_size=32, epochs=50, l2_reg=1e-4):
        self.lr = lr
        self.batch_size = batch_size
        self.epochs = epochs
        self.l2_reg = l2_reg
        self.w = None

    def fit_normal_equation(self, X, y):
        """Analytical Ridge OLS solution: w = (X^T X + lambda I)^-1 X^T y"""
        X_b = np.c_[np.ones((X.shape[0], 1)), X] # Add bias column
        d = X_b.shape[1]
        I = np.eye(d)
        I[0, 0] = 0.0 # Do not regularize bias!
        self.w = np.linalg.solve(X_b.T @ X_b + self.l2_reg * I, X_b.T @ y)

    def fit_sgd(self, X, y):
        """Mini-Batch Stochastic Gradient Descent"""
        N, d = X.shape
        X_b = np.c_[np.ones((N, 1)), X]
        self.w = np.zeros(d + 1)

        for epoch in range(self.epochs):
            indices = np.random.permutation(N)
            for start_idx in range(0, N, self.batch_size):
                batch_idx = indices[start_idx:start_idx + self.batch_size]
                X_batch = X_b[batch_idx]
                y_batch = y[batch_idx]

                # Prediction & Error
                preds = X_batch @ self.w
                errors = preds - y_batch

                # Gradient: (1/B) * X^T (Xw - y) + lambda * w
                grad = (X_batch.T @ errors) / len(batch_idx)
                grad[1:] += self.l2_reg * self.w[1:] # Regularize weights only

                self.w -= self.lr * grad

    def predict(self, X):
        X_b = np.c_[np.ones((X.shape[0], 1)), X]
        return X_b @ self.w

if __name__ == "__main__":
    np.random.seed(42)
    X = 2 * np.random.rand(100, 3)
    y = 4 + 3 * X[:, 0] + 1.5 * X[:, 1] - 2 * X[:, 2] + np.random.randn(100) * 0.1

    model = LinearRegressionScratch(lr=0.05, epochs=100)
    model.fit_normal_equation(X, y)
    print("OLS Normal Equations Weights:", np.round(model.w, 4))

    model_sgd = LinearRegressionScratch(lr=0.05, epochs=200)
    model_sgd.fit_sgd(X, y)
    print("Mini-Batch SGD Weights      :", np.round(model_sgd.w, 4))

Logistic Regression & Maximum Likelihood

Odds Ratios, The Sigmoid Identity, BCE Loss, IRLS & Softmax Classification ✦

"Prediction is very difficult, especially if it's about the future."

— Niels Bohr

Foundation • Core Pillar

1. From Linear Output to Calibrated Probability

Why can we not simply use linear regression $y = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b$ for binary classification ($y \in \{0, 1\}$)?

  1. Unbounded Range: A linear combination $\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b$ maps to $(-\infty, +\infty)$. For extreme feature values, it predicts values like $-1.8$ or $+2.4$, violating the fundamental Kolmogorov axioms of probability.
  2. Distortion by Outliers: Squaring errors on points that are extremely well classified (e.g., $y=1$ and $\hat{y}=4.0$) exerts a massive penalty $(4.0 - 1.0)^2 = 9.0$, forcing the decision boundary to rotate and corrupting classification accuracy on borderline points.

The Log-Odds (Logit) Transformation

To map a bounded probability $p \in (0, 1)$ smoothly onto the entire real line $(-\infty, +\infty)$, we first define the Odds Ratio—the ratio of success probability to failure probability:

$$\text{Odds} = \frac{p}{1 - p} \in (0, +\infty)$$

Taking the natural logarithm yields the Logit (Log-Odds) function:

$$\text{logit}(p) = \ln\left(\frac{p}{1 - p}\right) = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b$$

Solving algebraically for $p$:

$$\frac{p}{1 - p} = e^{\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b} \implies p = e^{\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b} (1 - p) = e^{\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b} - p e^{\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b}$$ $$p (1 + e^{\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b}) = e^{\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b} \implies p = \frac{e^{\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b}}{1 + e^{\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b)}} = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b)$$

This derives the Sigmoid (Logistic) Function $\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$!

The Crucial Sigmoid Derivative Identity:

$$\sigma'(z) = \frac{d}{dz} (1 + e^{-z})^{-1} = -(1 + e^{-z})^{-2} (-e^{-z}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} \cdot \frac{e^{-z}}{1 + e^{-z}} = \sigma(z) (1 - \sigma(z))$$

The derivative of the sigmoid is simply its own output multiplied by $(1 - \text{output})$!

2. Maximum Likelihood & Binary Cross-Entropy Loss

Assuming independent training samples, the likelihood of observing binary targets $y_i \in \{0, 1\}$ with predicted probabilities $p_i = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}_i)$ is modeled by the Bernoulli PMF:

$$L(\mathbf{w}) = \prod_{i=1}^N P(y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i; \mathbf{w}) = \prod_{i=1}^N p_i^{y_i} (1 - p_i)^{1 - y_i}$$

Taking the natural logarithm and dividing by $-N$ yields the Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) Loss:

$$\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}) = -\frac{1}{N} \ln L(\mathbf{w}) = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left[ y_i \ln(p_i) + (1 - y_i) \ln(1 - p_i) \right]$$

Deriving the Gradient Vector

Let $z_i = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}_i$. Applying the multivariable chain rule:

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{w}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_i}{\partial p_i} \frac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_i} \frac{\partial z_i}{\partial \mathbf{w}}$$
  • $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_i}{\partial p_i} = -\frac{y_i}{p_i} + \frac{1 - y_i}{1 - p_i} = \frac{p_i - y_i}{p_i (1 - p_i)}$
  • $\frac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_i} = p_i (1 - p_i)$
  • $\frac{\partial z_i}{\partial \mathbf{w}} = \mathbf{x}_i$

Notice how the term $p_i(1 - p_i)$ in the denominator cancels out with the sigmoid derivative:

$$\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left( \frac{p_i - y_i}{p_i(1-p_i)} \right) \left( p_i(1-p_i) \right) \mathbf{x}_i = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (p_i - y_i) \mathbf{x}_i$$

In matrix notation:

$$\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{N} \mathbf{X}^T (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y})$$

This matches the algebraic form of the linear regression gradient $\frac{1}{N} \mathbf{X}^T (\hat{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{y})$!

3. Second-Order Optimization: Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS)

First-order gradient descent updates weights as $\mathbf{w}^{(t+1)} = \mathbf{w}^{(t)} - \eta \nabla \mathcal{L}$. However, because Logistic Regression is twice-differentiable and strictly convex, we can apply Newton's Method to converge quadratically in 5 to 8 steps:

$$\mathbf{w}^{(t+1)} = \mathbf{w}^{(t)} - \mathbf{H}^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}^{(t)})$$

Recall the Hessian matrix derived in Problem 2.3.1:

$$\mathbf{H} = \frac{1}{N} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{D} \mathbf{X}, \quad \text{where } \mathbf{D} = \text{diag}(p_1(1-p_1), \dots, p_N(1-p_N))$$

Substituting the gradient and Hessian into Newton's update:

$$\mathbf{w}^{(t+1)} = \mathbf{w}^{(t)} - (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{D} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y})$$ $$\mathbf{w}^{(t+1)} = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{D} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \left[ \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{D} \mathbf{X} \mathbf{w}^{(t)} - \mathbf{X}^T (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y}) \right] = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{D} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{D} \left[ \mathbf{X} \mathbf{w}^{(t)} - \mathbf{D}^{-1}(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y}) \right]$$

Define the adjusted response vector $\mathbf{z}^{(t)} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}^{(t)} - \mathbf{D}^{-1}(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y})$. Then:

$$\mathbf{w}^{(t+1)} = (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{D} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{D} \mathbf{z}^{(t)}$$

Notice that this is the exact closed-form solution to a Weighted Least Squares (WLS) problem with diagonal weight matrix $\mathbf{D}$! Because the weights $\mathbf{D}$ depend on the current predictions $\mathbf{p}^{(t)}$, the weights must be recomputed on every step—hence the name Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS).

4. Multi-Class Generalization: Softmax (Multinomial) Regression

For $K > 2$ mutually exclusive classes, target labels are one-hot vectors $\mathbf{y}_i \in \{0, 1\}^K$. The model maintains a weight vector $\mathbf{w}_k$ for each class, computing class logits $z_{ik} = \mathbf{w}_k^T \mathbf{x}_i$. The probability distribution over classes is given by the Softmax Function:

$$P(y_i = k \mid \mathbf{x}_i) = p_{ik} = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{w}_k^T \mathbf{x}_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^K \exp(\mathbf{w}_j^T \mathbf{x}_i)}$$

The Multi-Class Categorical Cross-Entropy loss is:

$$\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{W}) = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K y_{ik} \ln(p_{ik})$$

The gradient with respect to class weight vector $\mathbf{w}_k$ is:

$$\nabla_{\mathbf{w}_k} \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (p_{ik} - y_{ik}) \mathbf{x}_i \implies \nabla_{\mathbf{W}} \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{N} \mathbf{X}^T (\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{Y})$$

Tier 1: Direct Formula & Numerical Warm-Up Drills

Problem 2.3.1 Easy Google

QUESTION: A trained binary logistic regression model has parameter vector $\mathbf{w} = [b, w_1, w_2]^T = [-2.0, 0.8, -0.5]^T$.

  1. For an incoming user profile with features $\mathbf{x} = [x_1, x_2]^T = [3.0, 2.0]^T$, compute the logit $z$, the odds ratio, and the predicted probability of conversion $p$.
  2. If feature $x_1$ increases by $+2.0$ units while $x_2$ remains unchanged, by what multiplicative factor does the odds ratio change?
✓ Complete Step-by-Step Numerical Solution

Step 1: Compute Logit, Odds, and Probability:
Compute the linear combination: $$z = b + w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 = -2.0 + (0.8 \times 3.0) + (-0.5 \times 2.0) = -2.0 + 2.4 - 1.0 = \mathbf{-0.60}$$ Compute Odds Ratio: $$\text{Odds} = e^z = e^{-0.60} \approx \mathbf{0.5488}$$ Compute Predicted Probability via Sigmoid: $$p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{0.60}} = \frac{1}{1 + 1.8221} = \frac{1}{2.8221} \approx \mathbf{0.3543} \quad (35.43\%)$$

Step 2: Odds Ratio Multiplicative Factor:
In logistic regression, the change in log-odds resulting from an increase of $\Delta x_1$ is $\Delta z = w_1 \Delta x_1$.
Here $\Delta x_1 = 2.0$ and $w_1 = 0.8$: $$\Delta z = 0.8 \times 2.0 = 1.60$$ The odds ratio scales by $e^{\Delta z}$: $$\text{Factor} = e^{1.60} \approx \mathbf{4.953}$$ Result: Increasing $x_1$ by 2.0 multiplies the odds of conversion by approximately $4.95\times$.

Problem 2.3.2 Easy Meta

QUESTION: Consider a dataset of $N=2$ samples: $$\mathbf{x}_1 = [1.0, 2.0]^T, \ y_1 = 1; \qquad \mathbf{x}_2 = [1.0, -1.0]^T, \ y_2 = 0$$ (where the first entry is the bias feature $x_0 = 1.0$). At initial weights $\mathbf{w}^{(0)} = [0.0, 0.0]^T$:

  1. Compute the initial predicted probabilities $p_1$ and $p_2$.
  2. Compute the initial Binary Cross-Entropy loss $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}^{(0)})$.
  3. Compute the exact gradient vector $\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}^{(0)})$.
✓ Complete Step-by-Step Numerical Solution

Step 1: Initial Predicted Probabilities:
For both samples, $z_1 = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}_1 = 0.0$ and $z_2 = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}_2 = 0.0$. $$p_1 = \sigma(0) = \frac{1}{1 + e^0} = \mathbf{0.50}, \qquad p_2 = \sigma(0) = \mathbf{0.50}$$

Step 2: Initial Binary Cross-Entropy Loss: $$\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{2} \left[ y_1 \ln(p_1) + (1-y_1)\ln(1-p_1) + y_2 \ln(p_2) + (1-y_2)\ln(1-p_2) \right]$$ $$\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{2} \left[ 1 \ln(0.5) + 0 + 0 + 1 \ln(0.5) \right] = -\ln(0.5) = \ln(2) \approx \mathbf{0.69315 \text{ nats}}$$

Step 3: Evaluate Gradient Vector:
Using $\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (p_i - y_i) \mathbf{x}_i$: $$p_1 - y_1 = 0.50 - 1.0 = -0.50$$ $$p_2 - y_2 = 0.50 - 0.0 = +0.50$$ Sum the weighted feature vectors: $$\nabla \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2} \left[ (-0.50) \begin{bmatrix} 1.0 \\ 2.0 \end{bmatrix} + (+0.50) \begin{bmatrix} 1.0 \\ -1.0 \end{bmatrix} \right] = \frac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} -0.50 + 0.50 \\ -1.00 - 0.50 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 0.0 \\ -1.50 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 0.0 \\ -0.75 \end{bmatrix}}$$ Result: The gradient indicates that the bias is currently balanced ($\nabla_b = 0$), while $w_1$ should be increased in the positive direction ($-\eta \nabla_{w_1} > 0$).

Tier 2: Applied Engineering & Algorithmic Tracing

Problem 2.3.3 Medium Apple

QUESTION: Trace one complete iteration of the Newton-Raphson / IRLS algorithm for the 2-sample dataset in Problem 2.3.2, starting from $\mathbf{w}^{(0)} = [0.0, 0.0]^T$.

$$\mathbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix} 1.0 & 2.0 \\ 1.0 & -1.0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$
  1. Compute the diagonal weight matrix $\mathbf{D} = \text{diag}(p_1(1-p_1), p_2(1-p_2))$.
  2. Compute the $2 \times 2$ Hessian matrix $\mathbf{H} = \frac{1}{N} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{D} \mathbf{X}$.
  3. Invert $\mathbf{H}$ and compute the Newton-Raphson updated weights $\mathbf{w}^{(1)} = \mathbf{w}^{(0)} - \mathbf{H}^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L}$.
✓ Complete Step-by-Step Algorithmic Trace

Step 1: Compute Diagonal Weight Matrix $\mathbf{D}$:
From Problem 2.3.2, $p_1 = 0.50$ and $p_2 = 0.50$: $$D_{11} = 0.5(1 - 0.5) = 0.25, \qquad D_{22} = 0.5(1 - 0.5) = 0.25$$ $$\mathbf{D} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.25 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.25 \end{bmatrix} = 0.25 \mathbf{I}_2$$

Step 2: Compute the Hessian Matrix $\mathbf{H}$:
With $N=2$: $$\mathbf{H} = \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{D} \mathbf{X} = \frac{0.25}{2} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} = \frac{1}{8} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}$$ Compute $\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}$: $$\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} = \begin{bmatrix} 1.0 & 1.0 \\ 2.0 & -1.0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1.0 & 2.0 \\ 1.0 & -1.0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1+1 & 2-1 \\ 2-1 & 4+1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ Therefore: $$\mathbf{H} = \frac{1}{8} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.250 & 0.125 \\ 0.125 & 0.625 \end{bmatrix}$$

Step 3: Invert $\mathbf{H}$ and Update $\mathbf{w}$:
$$\det(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X}) = (2)(5) - (1)(1) = 9 \implies \det(\mathbf{H}) = \frac{9}{64}$$ $$\mathbf{H}^{-1} = 8 (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} = \frac{8}{9} \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ From Problem 2.3.2, the gradient is $\nabla \mathcal{L} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.0 \\ -0.75 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -3/4 \end{bmatrix}$.
Evaluate the Newton step $\mathbf{H}^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L}$: $$\mathbf{H}^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L} = \frac{8}{9} \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -3/4 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{8}{9} \begin{bmatrix} 3/4 \\ -6/4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2/3 \\ -4/3 \end{bmatrix}$$ Update weights: $$\mathbf{w}^{(1)} = \mathbf{w}^{(0)} - \mathbf{H}^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 2/3 \\ -4/3 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} -2/3 \\ +4/3 \end{bmatrix}} \approx \begin{bmatrix} -0.6667 \\ +1.3333 \end{bmatrix}$$ Verification of Improvement:
Compute new logits: $z_1 = -2/3 + 4/3(2) = 6/3 = +2.0 \implies p_1 = \sigma(2.0) \approx 0.8808$ (True class was 1!).
$z_2 = -2/3 + 4/3(-1) = -6/3 = -2.0 \implies p_2 = \sigma(-2.0) \approx 0.1192$ (True class was 0!).
Result: In a single Newton step, probability for sample 1 jumped from $0.50$ to $0.88$, and sample 2 dropped from $0.50$ to $0.12$!

Problem 2.3.4 Medium Amazon

QUESTION: An autonomous vehicle perception model outputs probability estimates for pedestrian detection. An empirical audit over 5 validation bins reveals the following predicted vs empirical probabilities:

Bin $m$Bin RangeAvg Confidence $\text{conf}(B_m)$Empirical Accuracy $\text{acc}(B_m)$Bin Size $|B_m|$
1$[0.0, 0.2)$$0.10$$0.12$$200$
2$[0.2, 0.4)$$0.30$$0.35$$300$
3$[0.4, 0.6)$$0.50$$0.48$$250$
4$[0.6, 0.8)$$0.70$$0.60$$150$
5$[0.8, 1.0]$$0.90$$0.75$$100$

Total validation samples $N = 1,000$. Compute the Expected Calibration Error (ECE): $$\text{ECE} = \sum_{m=1}^M \frac{|B_m|}{N} \left| \text{acc}(B_m) - \text{conf}(B_m) \right|$$

✓ Complete Step-by-Step Numerical Solution

Step 1: Compute Calibration Error per Bin:

  • Bin 1 ($|B_1| = 200$, weight $0.20$): $|0.12 - 0.10| = 0.02 \implies 0.20 \times 0.02 = 0.0040$
  • Bin 2 ($|B_2| = 300$, weight $0.30$): $|0.35 - 0.30| = 0.05 \implies 0.30 \times 0.05 = 0.0150$
  • Bin 3 ($|B_3| = 250$, weight $0.25$): $|0.48 - 0.50| = 0.02 \implies 0.25 \times 0.02 = 0.0050$
  • Bin 4 ($|B_4| = 150$, weight $0.15$): $|0.60 - 0.70| = 0.10 \implies 0.15 \times 0.10 = 0.0150$
  • Bin 5 ($|B_5| = 100$, weight $0.10$): $|0.75 - 0.90| = 0.15 \implies 0.10 \times 0.15 = 0.0150$

Step 2: Sum Weighted Errors: $$\text{ECE} = 0.0040 + 0.0150 + 0.0050 + 0.0150 + 0.0150 = \mathbf{0.0540} \quad (5.40\%)$$ Result: The model's Expected Calibration Error is $5.4\%$. In high-confidence bins ($B_4, B_5$), the model is significantly overconfident ($\text{conf} > \text{acc}$), necessitating temperature scaling.

Tier 3: FAANG & Research Lab Challenges

Problem 2.3.5 Hard Google Brain Meta FAIR

QUESTION: For Multi-Class Softmax Regression with $K$ classes, class probabilities are given by: $$p_k = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{w}_k^T \mathbf{x})}{\sum_{j=1}^K \exp(\mathbf{w}_j^T \mathbf{x})}$$

  1. Derive the partial derivative of class probability $p_i$ with respect to logit $z_j = \mathbf{w}_j^T \mathbf{x}$, proving: $$\frac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_j} = p_i (\delta_{ij} - p_j)$$ where $\delta_{ij}$ is the Kronecker delta.
  2. Using this identity, derive the complete gradient of the Cross-Entropy loss $\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{k=1}^K y_k \ln(p_k)$ with respect to the weight vector $\mathbf{w}_j$, proving $\nabla_{\mathbf{w}_j} \mathcal{L} = (p_j - y_j)\mathbf{x}$.
✓ Complete Step-by-Step Mathematical Derivation

Step 1: Differentiate Softmax with Respect to Logits:
Let $S = \sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j}$. Then $p_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{S}$.
Apply the quotient rule $\frac{d}{dz_j} [u/v] = \frac{u' v - u v'}{v^2}$:

  • Case 1 ($i = j$): $$\frac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_i} = \frac{(e^{z_i}) S - (e^{z_i})(e^{z_i})}{S^2} = \frac{e^{z_i}}{S} - \left(\frac{e^{z_i}}{S}\right)^2 = p_i - p_i^2 = p_i(1 - p_i)$$
  • Case 2 ($i \neq j$): $$\frac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_j} = \frac{(0) S - (e^{z_i})(e^{z_j})}{S^2} = -\frac{e^{z_i}}{S} \cdot \frac{e^{z_j}}{S} = -p_i p_j$$
Combining both cases using the Kronecker delta $\delta_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i=j \\ 0 & \text{if } i \neq j \end{cases}$: $$\frac{\partial p_i}{\partial z_j} = p_i (\delta_{ij} - p_j)$$

Step 2: Differentiate Cross-Entropy Loss:
$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_j} = \sum_{k=1}^K \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial p_k} \frac{\partial p_k}{\partial z_j}$$ Since $\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{k=1}^K y_k \ln(p_k)$, we have $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial p_k} = -\frac{y_k}{p_k}$.
Substitute into the sum: $$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_j} = \sum_{k=1}^K \left(-\frac{y_k}{p_k}\right) \left[ p_k (\delta_{kj} - p_j) \right] = -\sum_{k=1}^K y_k (\delta_{kj} - p_j) = -\sum_{k=1}^K y_k \delta_{kj} + p_j \sum_{k=1}^K y_k$$ Since $\mathbf{y}$ is a one-hot distribution, $\sum_{k=1}^K y_k = 1$, and $\sum_{k=1}^K y_k \delta_{kj} = y_j$: $$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_j} = -y_j + p_j(1) = \mathbf{p_j - y_j}$$ Now apply chain rule to weight vector $\mathbf{w}_j$ ($z_j = \mathbf{w}_j^T \mathbf{x} \implies \frac{\partial z_j}{\partial \mathbf{w}_j} = \mathbf{x}$): $$\nabla_{\mathbf{w}_j} \mathcal{L} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_j} \frac{\partial z_j}{\partial \mathbf{w}_j} = \mathbf{(p_j - y_j) \mathbf{x}}$$ Q.E.D. The multi-class gradient for class $j$ is simply the prediction residual $(p_j - y_j)$ times the feature vector $\mathbf{x}$!

Problem 2.3.6 Hard DeepMind

QUESTION: The Separation Problem (Hauck-Donner Effect): Suppose a binary dataset is strictly linearly separable, meaning there exists a hyperplane $(\mathbf{w}^*, b^*)$ such that $y_i(\mathbf{w}^{*T} \mathbf{x}_i + b^*) > 0$ for all $i=1,\dots,N$.

  1. Prove that the Maximum Likelihood estimator $\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{MLE}}$ does not exist at any finite coordinates ($\|\hat{\mathbf{w}}_{\text{MLE}}\|_2 \to \infty$).
  2. Explain the practical engineering danger of this phenomenon in deep learning and logistic regression pipelines, and prove how $L_2$ regularization mathematically cures it.
✓ Complete Step-by-Step Mathematical Proof

Step 1: Divergence of MLE on Separable Data:
If data is strictly separable, scaling the separating vector by an arbitrary positive scalar $c > 0$ ($\mathbf{w} = c \mathbf{w}^*$) maintains perfect separation.
Examine the predicted probabilities for positive points ($y_i = 1$): $$p_i(c) = \sigma(c (\mathbf{w}^{*T} \mathbf{x}_i + b^*)) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-c \cdot \Delta_i}}, \quad \text{where } \Delta_i = (\mathbf{w}^{*T} \mathbf{x}_i + b^*) > 0$$ As $c \to \infty$, $e^{-c \Delta_i} \to 0$, so $p_i(c) \to 1.0$.
Similarly for negative points ($y_i = 0$), $p_i(c) \to 0.0 \implies (1 - p_i(c)) \to 1.0$.
Examine the Negative Log-Likelihood: $$\lim_{c \to \infty} \mathcal{L}(c \mathbf{w}^*) = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \left[ y_i \ln(1) + (1-y_i) \ln(1) \right] = 0$$ The infimum of the loss is $0$, but this loss is never attained for any finite weights $\mathbf{w}$! Any optimization algorithm (gradient descent) will run indefinitely, pushing weights toward $\infty$.

Step 2: Engineering Impact & $L_2$ Regularization Cure:
As $\|\mathbf{w}\| \to \infty$:

  • Probabilities saturate at $0.0$ and $1.0$. The model becomes severely overconfident and uncalibrated.
  • The sigmoid derivative $\sigma'(z) \to 0$, causing vanishing gradients.
  • Standard errors of weights explode, triggering numerical instability in Wald tests (the Hauck-Donner effect).
Adding $L_2$ regularization creates a penalized objective: $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{Ridge}}(\mathbf{w}) = \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}) + \frac{\lambda}{2} \|\mathbf{w}\|_2^2$$ As $\|\mathbf{w}\| \to \infty$, the penalty $\frac{\lambda}{2} \|\mathbf{w}\|_2^2 \to \infty$. By the Extreme Value Theorem, the penalized objective is coercive and strictly convex, guaranteeing a unique finite global minimum $\mathbf{w}^*_{\text{reg}}$!

Tier 4: Conceptual Trap MCQs & Assertion-Reasoning

Problem 2.3.7 Medium Google

QUESTION: Both Logistic Regression and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) produce linear decision boundaries in feature space. Which of the following statements correctly captures their key mathematical difference?

  1. Logistic Regression is a generative model that assumes features are Gaussian, whereas LDA is a discriminative model that makes no distributional assumptions.
  2. LDA is a generative model that assumes features $\mathbf{x} \mid y$ follow multivariate normal distributions with shared covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, whereas Logistic Regression is a discriminative model that makes no assumptions about feature distributions.
  3. Logistic Regression cannot handle more than 2 classes, whereas LDA generalizes to arbitrary numbers of classes.
  4. LDA minimizes cross-entropy loss, whereas Logistic Regression minimizes hinge loss.
✓ Complete Conceptual Analysis & Explanation

Correct Option: B

Exhaustive Analysis of All Options:

  • Option B is TRUE: LDA models the joint probability $P(\mathbf{x}, y) = P(\mathbf{x} \mid y) P(y)$, assuming $P(\mathbf{x} \mid y=k) \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})$ with an identical shared covariance matrix across all classes. Under these Gaussian assumptions, Bayes' rule yields linear log-odds. Logistic Regression is discriminative: it models $P(y \mid \mathbf{x})$ directly without making any assumptions about $P(\mathbf{x})$ (features can be binary, skewed, categorical, or multimodal).
  • Option A is FALSE: Exactly backwards; LDA is generative, Logistic Regression is discriminative.
  • Option C is FALSE: Softmax regression seamlessly generalizes Logistic Regression to $K$ classes.
  • Option D is FALSE: LDA is fit via sample means and pooled covariance matrices (plug-in estimates); Hinge loss is minimized by Support Vector Machines.

Problem 2.3.8 Hard Microsoft

QUESTION: Consider the following Assertion (A) and Reason (R):

Assertion (A): When training unregularized binary logistic regression via gradient descent on a dataset where one class is completely linearly separable from the other, the training loss approaches zero, but the model's predicted probabilities will become increasingly uncalibrated over epochs.

Reason (R): Because the gradient $\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{N} \mathbf{X}^T (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y})$ drives all probabilities toward $p_i \to y_i \in \{0, 1\}$, the weight vector norm $\|\mathbf{w}\|_2$ grows without bound, artificially pushing all sigmoid inputs into saturated extremes.

  1. Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
  2. Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
  3. (A) is true, but (R) is false.
  4. (A) is false, but (R) is true.
✓ Complete Conceptual Analysis & Explanation

Correct Option: A

Exhaustive Analysis of Assertion & Reason:

  • Assertion (A) is TRUE: As proven in Problem 2.3.6, on separable data, unregularized gradient descent continues pushing weights toward infinity ($\|\mathbf{w}\| \to \infty$) to reduce loss from $0.001$ to $0.0001$. As a result, the model assigns probabilities of $0.99999$ or $0.00001$ even to points that lie very close to the decision boundary, destroying probability calibration.
  • Reason (R) is TRUE: The gradient is driven by the residual $(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y})$. Since $p_i = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}_i) = 1$ is only achieved at $z \to \infty$, the gradient can never equal zero at any finite point. The optimizer continues stepping in the direction of the separating vector, driving $\|\mathbf{w}\| \to \infty$.
  • Furthermore, Reason (R) is the precise mathematical mechanism causing Assertion (A).

5. Production Code Lab 2.3: Logistic Regression with Newton-Raphson IRLS

Below is a production Python implementation comparing first-order Gradient Descent against the second-order Newton-Raphson (IRLS) solver.

Code Lab 2.3 — Logistic Regression & Second-Order IRLS Solver

🔗 View in GitHub: part2_classical_ml/ch23_logistic_regression/logistic_regression_scratch.py

import numpy as np

class LogisticRegressionIRLS:
    def __init__(self, max_iter=20, tol=1e-6):
        self.max_iter = max_iter
        self.tol = tol
        self.w = None

    def _sigmoid(self, z):
        return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-np.clip(z, -250, 250)))

    def fit(self, X, y):
        N, d = X.shape
        X_b = np.c_[np.ones((N, 1)), X]
        self.w = np.zeros(d + 1)

        for iteration in range(self.max_iter):
            p = self._sigmoid(X_b @ self.w)
            
            # Gradient: (1/N) * X^T (p - y)
            grad = (X_b.T @ (p - y)) / N

            # Hessian: (1/N) * X^T D X, where D = p * (1 - p)
            D = p * (1.0 - p)
            # Efficient computation without allocating NxN diagonal matrix:
            H = (X_b.T * D) @ X_b / N + 1e-5 * np.eye(d + 1) # Regularization for invertibility

            # Newton-Raphson update: w = w - H^-1 * grad
            delta_w = np.linalg.solve(H, grad)
            self.w -= delta_w

            if np.linalg.norm(delta_w) < self.tol:
                print(f"Newton-Raphson converged in {iteration+1} iterations!")
                break

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        X_b = np.c_[np.ones((X.shape[0], 1)), X]
        return self._sigmoid(X_b @ self.w)

    def predict(self, X, threshold=0.5):
        return (self.predict_proba(X) >= threshold).astype(int)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    np.random.seed(42)
    # Generate 2D separable synthetic classification data
    X1 = np.random.randn(100, 2) + np.array([2.0, 2.0])
    X2 = np.random.randn(100, 2) + np.array([-2.0, -2.0])
    X = np.vstack([X1, X2])
    y = np.array([1]*100 + [0]*100)

    model = LogisticRegressionIRLS()
    model.fit(X, y)
    print("Fitted Weights [b, w1, w2]:", np.round(model.w, 4))
    
    preds = model.predict(X)
    acc = np.mean(preds == y)
    print(f"Classification Accuracy   : {acc * 100:.1f}%")

Chapter 2.4

Decision Trees & Information Gain

CART, Gini Impurity, Variance Reduction, Cost-Complexity Pruning & Axis-Aligned Geometry ✦

"In a forest of a hundred thousand trees, no two leaves are alike. And no two journeys along the same path are alike."

— Paulo Coelho

Foundation • Core Pillar

1. The Recursive Axis-Aligned Partitioning Paradigm

Linear models divide the feature space with a single flat hyperplane ($\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b = 0$). While computationally efficient, linear boundaries fail on non-linear geometries (such as the XOR problem or concentric circles) without manual polynomial feature expansion.

Decision Trees abandon the global parametric assumption entirely. Instead, they apply a greedy, top-down recursive partitioning strategy that divides the feature space $\mathbb{R}^d$ into a collection of mutually exclusive hyper-rectangles using axis-aligned orthogonal cuts ($x_j \le \theta$):

$$\hat{y}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{m=1}^{|T|} c_m \mathbb{I}(\mathbf{x} \in R_m)$$

where $R_m$ is region $m$ associated with leaf node $m$, and $c_m$ is the leaf output:

  • Classification: Plurality vote (majority class) $c_m = \arg\max_k \sum_{\mathbf{x}_i \in R_m} \mathbb{I}(y_i = k)$, or empirical class probability distribution $p_{mk} = \frac{1}{|R_m|} \sum_{\mathbf{x}_i \in R_m} \mathbb{I}(y_i = k)$.
  • Regression: Under squared loss ($L_2$), the optimal constant prediction is the sample mean $c_m = \frac{1}{|R_m|} \sum_{\mathbf{x}_i \in R_m} y_i$. Under absolute loss ($L_1$), the optimal prediction is the sample median $c_m = \text{median}(\{y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i \in R_m\})$.

2. Splitting Criteria: Classification & Regression

At each internal node, the tree must choose the feature $j$ and split threshold $\theta$ that maximizes the purity of the resulting child nodes.

Splitting Criterion Task Mathematical Formula Computational Characteristics
Gini Impurity Classification $I_G(S) = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^K p_k^2$ Fastest ($1$ CPU cycle per evaluation). Default in CART / scikit-learn.
Shannon Entropy Classification $H(S) = -\sum_{k=1}^K p_k \log_2(p_k)$ Slower ($20\text{--}50$ CPU cycles for transcendentals). Strongly penalizes impure nodes. Used in ID3 / C4.5.
Misclassification Error Classification $E(S) = 1 - \max_k p_k$ Not strictly concave; poor for tree growth because it fails to reward purity improvements off the majority class.
Variance Reduction (MSE) Regression $I_{\text{Var}}(S) = \frac{1}{|S|} \sum_{i \in S} (y_i - \bar{y}_S)^2$ Standard $L_2$ regression split. Equivalent to maximizing child separation: $\frac{N_L N_R}{N} (\bar{y}_L - \bar{y}_R)^2$.

The Information Gain Formula

When a candidate split partitions dataset $S$ of size $N$ into Left subset $S_L$ of size $N_L$ and Right subset $S_R$ of size $N_R$, the Information Gain is the reduction in impurity:

$$\Delta I = I(S) - \left[ \frac{N_L}{N} I(S_L) + \frac{N_R}{N} I(S_R) \right]$$

Because the impurity functions (Gini and Entropy) are strictly concave functions of the probability vector $\mathbf{p}$, Jensen's inequality guarantees that $\Delta I \ge 0$ always: splitting a node can never increase impurity!

3. Overfitting & Minimal Cost-Complexity Pruning

An unconstrained decision tree will grow until every training point sits in its own isolated leaf node ($100\%$ training accuracy, zero bias). However, such trees suffer from massive variance, capturing random data noise rather than structural signal.

Minimal Cost-Complexity Pruning ($L_0$ Regularization)

Breiman et al. introduced Cost-Complexity Pruning, defining a regularized loss function that balances training misclassification rate $\mathcal{R}(T)$ with tree complexity (number of terminal leaves $|T|$):

$$\mathcal{R}_\alpha(T) = \mathcal{R}(T) + \alpha |T|$$

where $\alpha \ge 0$ is the complexity tuning parameter:

  • $\alpha = 0$: The original, unconstrained full tree $T_{\max}$.
  • $\alpha \to \infty$: The simplest possible tree (a single root node).

For every internal node $t$, collapsing its entire descendant subtree $T_t$ into a single leaf increases empirical error by $\mathcal{R}(t) - \mathcal{R}(T_t)$ while reducing leaf count by $|T_t| - 1$. The effective cost-complexity threshold is:

$$\alpha_{\text{eff}}(t) = \frac{\mathcal{R}(t) - \mathcal{R}(T_t)}{|T_t| - 1}$$

Pruning the node with the smallest $\alpha_{\text{eff}}$ produces a finite, nested hierarchy of optimal subtrees $T_0 \supset T_1 \supset T_2 \supset \dots \supset \{\text{root}\}$, from which the optimal subtree is selected via cross-validation.

Tier 1: Direct Formula & Numerical Warm-Up Drills

Problem 2.4.1 Easy Google Amazon

QUESTION: A dataset at node $S$ contains $N = 20$ samples across 3 classes: $$N_A = 10, \quad N_B = 6, \quad N_C = 4$$ Compute step-by-step:

  1. The class probability distribution $\mathbf{p} = [p_A, p_B, p_C]$.
  2. The Gini Impurity $I_G(S)$.
  3. The Shannon Entropy $H(S)$ in bits.
  4. The Misclassification Error $E(S)$.
✓ Complete Step-by-Step Numerical Solution

Step 1: Compute Probabilities: $$p_A = \frac{10}{20} = 0.50, \qquad p_B = \frac{6}{20} = 0.30, \qquad p_C = \frac{4}{20} = 0.20$$

Step 2: Compute Gini Impurity: $$I_G(S) = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^3 p_k^2 = 1 - \left( 0.50^2 + 0.30^2 + 0.20^2 \right)$$ $$I_G(S) = 1 - (0.25 + 0.09 + 0.04) = 1 - 0.38 = \mathbf{0.6200}$$

Step 3: Compute Shannon Entropy in Bits: $$H(S) = -\sum_{k=1}^3 p_k \log_2(p_k) = -\left[ 0.5 \log_2(0.5) + 0.3 \log_2(0.3) + 0.2 \log_2(0.2) \right]$$ $$\log_2(0.5) = -1.0, \quad \log_2(0.3) \approx -1.7370, \quad \log_2(0.2) \approx -2.3219$$ $$H(S) = -[0.5(-1.0) + 0.3(-1.7370) + 0.2(-2.3219)] = 0.50 + 0.5211 + 0.4644 = \mathbf{1.4855 \text{ bits}}$$

Step 4: Compute Misclassification Error: $$E(S) = 1 - \max(p_A, p_B, p_C) = 1 - 0.50 = \mathbf{0.5000}$$ Verification of ordering: $E(S) = 0.50 \le I_G(S) = 0.62 \le H(S) = 1.4855$.

Problem 2.4.2 Easy Meta

QUESTION: A regression tree node contains $N = 4$ target values: $\mathbf{y} = [2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0]$. A candidate split divides the samples into Left child $S_L = [2.0, 4.0]$ and Right child $S_R = [6.0, 8.0]$. Compute:

  1. The parent node variance $\text{Var}(S)$.
  2. The Left and Right child node variances $\text{Var}(S_L)$ and $\text{Var}(S_R)$.
  3. The Variance Reduction $\Delta \text{Var}$ achieved by this split.
✓ Complete Step-by-Step Numerical Solution

Step 1: Parent Node Variance:
Mean: $\bar{y} = \frac{2 + 4 + 6 + 8}{4} = 5.0$. $$\text{Var}(S) = \frac{(2-5)^2 + (4-5)^2 + (6-5)^2 + (8-5)^2}{4} = \frac{9 + 1 + 1 + 9}{4} = \frac{20}{4} = \mathbf{5.00}$$

Step 2: Child Node Variances:
Left Child ($S_L = [2.0, 4.0]$): Mean $\bar{y}_L = 3.0$. $$\text{Var}(S_L) = \frac{(2-3)^2 + (4-3)^2}{2} = \frac{1 + 1}{2} = \mathbf{1.00}$$ Right Child ($S_R = [6.0, 8.0]$): Mean $\bar{y}_R = 7.0$. $$\text{Var}(S_R) = \frac{(6-7)^2 + (8-7)^2}{2} = \frac{1 + 1}{2} = \mathbf{1.00}$$

Step 3: Compute Variance Reduction: $$\text{Weighted Child Variance} = \frac{2}{4}(1.00) + \frac{2}{4}(1.00) = 1.00$$ $$\Delta \text{Var} = \text{Var}(S) - \text{Weighted Child Variance} = 5.00 - 1.00 = \mathbf{4.00}$$ Cross-Check via Between-Group Separation: $$\Delta \text{Var} = \frac{N_L N_R}{N^2} (\bar{y}_L - \bar{y}_R)^2 = \frac{2 \times 2}{16} (3.0 - 7.0)^2 = \frac{1}{4} (-4.0)^2 = \frac{16}{4} = \mathbf{4.00} \quad \checkmark$$ Result: The split slashes variance by $80\%$, reducing variance from $5.0$ to $1.0$.

Tier 2: Applied Engineering & Algorithmic Tracing

Problem 2.4.3 Medium Apple

QUESTION: A binary classification dataset has a continuous feature $X_1$ and label $Y \in \{0, 1\}$:

Sample $i$12345
Feature $X_1$$1.0$$2.0$$3.0$$5.0$$6.0$
Label $Y$$0$$0$$1$$1$$0$

Trace the exact CART split selection for feature $X_1$:

  1. Identify all 4 candidate midpoint thresholds.
  2. Compute the weighted child Gini impurity for each candidate threshold.
  3. Select the optimal split threshold $\theta^*$ and compute its Information Gain $\Delta I_G$.
✓ Complete Step-by-Step Algorithmic Trace

Step 1: Identify Candidate Midpoints:
Unique sorted values: $1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0, 6.0$.
Midpoint candidate thresholds: $$\theta_1 = \frac{1+2}{2} = 1.5, \quad \theta_2 = \frac{2+3}{2} = 2.5, \quad \theta_3 = \frac{3+5}{2} = 4.0, \quad \theta_4 = \frac{5+6}{2} = 5.5$$ Parent labels: three $0$s, two $1$s ($N=5$). $$I_G(S) = 1 - \left( (3/5)^2 + (2/5)^2 \right) = 1 - (0.36 + 0.16) = 1 - 0.52 = 0.4800$$

Step 2: Evaluate All 4 Midpoints:

  • Threshold $\theta_1 = 1.5$:
    • Left ($X_1 \le 1.5$): $[0]$ ($N_L=1$, pure: $I_G = 0.0$).
    • Right ($X_1 > 1.5$): $[0, 1, 1, 0]$ ($N_R=4$, $p_0=0.5, p_1=0.5 \implies I_G = 0.50$).
    • Weighted Impurity: $\frac{1}{5}(0.0) + \frac{4}{5}(0.50) = 0.4000$.
  • Threshold $\theta_2 = 2.5$:
    • Left ($X_1 \le 2.5$): $[0, 0]$ ($N_L=2$, pure: $I_G = 0.0$).
    • Right ($X_1 > 2.5$): $[1, 1, 0]$ ($N_R=3$, $p_1 = 2/3, p_0 = 1/3 \implies I_G = 1 - (4/9 + 1/9) = 4/9 \approx 0.4444$).
    • Weighted Impurity: $\frac{2}{5}(0.0) + \frac{3}{5}\left(\frac{4}{9}\right) = \frac{12}{45} \approx \mathbf{0.2667}$.
  • Threshold $\theta_3 = 4.0$:
    • Left ($X_1 \le 4.0$): $[0, 0, 1]$ ($N_L=3$, $I_G = 4/9 \approx 0.4444$).
    • Right ($X_1 > 4.0$): $[1, 0]$ ($N_R=2$, $I_G = 0.50$).
    • Weighted Impurity: $\frac{3}{5}\left(\frac{4}{9}\right) + \frac{2}{5}(0.50) = \frac{4}{15} + 0.20 = 0.2667 + 0.20 = 0.4667$.
  • Threshold $\theta_4 = 5.5$:
    • Left ($X_1 \le 5.5$): $[0, 0, 1, 1]$ ($N_L=4$, $I_G = 0.50$).
    • Right ($X_1 > 5.5$): $[0]$ ($N_R=1$, pure: $I_G = 0.0$).
    • Weighted Impurity: $\frac{4}{5}(0.50) + \frac{1}{5}(0.0) = 0.4000$.

Step 3: Select the Optimal Split:
Threshold $\theta_2 = 2.5$ achieves the lowest weighted impurity ($0.2667$). $$\Delta I_G = 0.4800 - 0.2667 = \mathbf{0.2133}$$ Result: Optimal split is $X_1 \le 2.5$ with Information Gain $0.2133$.

Problem 2.4.4 Medium Amazon

QUESTION: In Cost-Complexity Pruning, an unpruned full tree $T_0$ has root node $t_0$ and an internal subtree $T_1$ with 3 terminal leaves ($|T_1| = 3$). Total validation samples $N = 100$.

  • If subtree $T_1$ is kept, the 3 leaves make a combined total of $R(T_1) = 4$ misclassification errors.
  • If subtree $T_1$ is collapsed into a single leaf node $t_1$, the single leaf makes $R(t_1) = 10$ misclassification errors.
Compute the effective pruning cost $\alpha_{\text{eff}}(t_1)$ for this node.

✓ Complete Step-by-Step Numerical Solution

Step 1: Compute Error Increase and Leaf Reduction:
Misclassification error rate increase: $$\Delta R = R(t_1) - R(T_1) = \frac{10}{100} - \frac{4}{100} = \frac{6}{100} = 0.06$$ Complexity leaf count reduction: $$\Delta |T| = |T_1| - 1 = 3 - 1 = 2 \text{ leaves}$$

Step 2: Evaluate Effective Alpha: $$\alpha_{\text{eff}}(t_1) = \frac{R(t_1) - R(T_1)}{|T_1| - 1} = \frac{0.06}{2} = \mathbf{0.030}$$ Interpretation: If the regularization penalty $\alpha$ in $\mathcal{R}_\alpha(T) = \mathcal{R}(T) + \alpha |T|$ exceeds $0.030$, pruning subtree $T_1$ reduces the total regularized cost, and the algorithm collapses it into a leaf.

Tier 3: FAANG & Research Lab Challenges

Problem 2.4.5 Hard Google DeepMind Meta FAIR

QUESTION: Prove rigorously from first principles that for any discrete probability distribution vector $\mathbf{p} = [p_1, \dots, p_K]$ on the probability simplex $\Delta^K$, both the Gini Impurity $I_G(\mathbf{p}) = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^K p_k^2$ and Shannon Entropy $H(\mathbf{p}) = -\sum_{k=1}^K p_k \ln(p_k)$ are strictly concave functions of $\mathbf{p}$. From this, apply Jensen's Inequality to prove that Information Gain is strictly non-negative ($\Delta I \ge 0$) for any split.

✓ Complete Step-by-Step Mathematical Proof

Step 1: Prove Concavity of Gini Impurity:
Compute the Hessian matrix of $I_G(\mathbf{p})$ with respect to $\mathbf{p}$:
First derivative: $\frac{\partial I_G}{\partial p_i} = -2 p_i$.
Second derivative: $$\frac{\partial^2 I_G}{\partial p_i \partial p_j} = -2 \delta_{ij} \implies \nabla^2 I_G(\mathbf{p}) = -2 \mathbf{I}_K$$ For any non-zero vector $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}$: $$\mathbf{v}^T \nabla^2 I_G(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{v} = -2 \|\mathbf{v}\|_2^2 < 0$$ The Hessian is strictly negative definite everywhere, proving that $I_G(\mathbf{p})$ is strictly concave.

Step 2: Prove Concavity of Shannon Entropy:
First derivative: $\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i} = -\ln(p_i) - 1$.
Second derivative: $$\frac{\partial^2 H}{\partial p_i \partial p_j} = -\frac{1}{p_i} \delta_{ij} \implies \nabla^2 H(\mathbf{p}) = -\text{diag}\left( \frac{1}{p_1}, \dots, \frac{1}{p_K} \right)$$ Since $p_k > 0$, all diagonal entries are strictly negative: $$\mathbf{v}^T \nabla^2 H(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{v} = -\sum_{k=1}^K \frac{v_k^2}{p_k} < 0, \quad \forall \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}$$ The Hessian is strictly negative definite, proving that $H(\mathbf{p})$ is strictly concave.

Step 3: Prove Information Gain $\Delta I \ge 0$ via Jensen's Inequality:
Let a split divide parent node $S$ (size $N$) into Left $S_L$ ($N_L$) and Right $S_R$ ($N_R$).
Notice that the parent class probability vector is the exact weighted average of child probability vectors: $$\mathbf{p}_S = \frac{N_L}{N} \mathbf{p}_L + \frac{N_R}{N} \mathbf{p}_R$$ Let $f(\mathbf{p})$ be any concave impurity measure ($I_G$ or $H$). By Jensen's Inequality for concave functions: $$f\left( \alpha \mathbf{p}_L + (1-\alpha)\mathbf{p}_R \right) \ge \alpha f(\mathbf{p}_L) + (1-\alpha) f(\mathbf{p}_R), \quad \text{where } \alpha = \frac{N_L}{N} \in [0, 1]$$ Substitute $\mathbf{p}_S$: $$f(\mathbf{p}_S) \ge \frac{N_L}{N} f(\mathbf{p}_L) + \frac{N_R}{N} f(\mathbf{p}_R)$$ Rearranging terms: $$\Delta I = f(\mathbf{p}_S) - \left[ \frac{N_L}{N} f(\mathbf{p}_L) + \frac{N_R}{N} f(\mathbf{p}_R) \right] \ge 0$$ Q.E.D. Because Gini and Entropy are concave, splitting a node is mathematically guaranteed to never increase impurity!

Problem 2.4.6 Hard Microsoft Apple

QUESTION: A categorical feature $X$ has $K$ unordered levels $\{c_1, \dots, c_K\}$.

  1. How many non-trivial binary partitions of these $K$ categories exist? Show that brute-force evaluation scales as $\mathcal{O}(2^K)$.
  2. Prove Fisher's Exact Splitting Theorem (Breiman et al., 1984) for binary classification: prove that sorting the categories by their empirical proportion of positive instances $p(y=1 \mid X=c_k)$ reduces the search space from $2^{K-1}-1$ to only $K-1$ splits, while guaranteeing the mathematically optimal Gini / Entropy split.
✓ Complete Step-by-Step Mathematical Proof

Step 1: Combinatorial Explosion of Categorical Splits:
A binary split partitions the $K$ categories into two non-empty disjoint subsets $A$ and $B$.
The number of non-empty subsets is $2^K - 2$. Because swapping subsets $A$ and $B$ produces the identical split, we divide by 2: $$\text{Number of Unique Binary Splits} = \frac{2^K - 2}{2} = 2^{K-1} - 1$$ For a zip-code or city feature with $K = 50$ categories, $2^{49} - 1 \approx 5.6 \times 10^{14}$ candidate splits! A brute-force search is completely impossible.

Step 2: Fisher's Theorem Proof:
For binary classification ($y \in \{0, 1\}$), let $\bar{y}_k = P(y = 1 \mid X = c_k)$ denote the proportion of positive labels in category $c_k$.
Sort the categories in ascending order of positive response rates: $$\bar{y}_{(1)} \le \bar{y}_{(2)} \le \dots \le \bar{y}_{(K)}$$ Breiman et al. (1984) proved that for any strictly concave impurity function $f$, the optimal subset split $A^*$ that maximizes impurity reduction must be an interval partition of this sorted sequence: $$A^* = \{c_{(1)}, c_{(2)}, \dots, c_{(m)}\} \quad \text{for some } 1 \le m \le K-1$$ Mathematical Intuition: If a partition contained a category with higher positive rate in subset $A$ and a category with lower positive rate in subset $B$, swapping them strictly increases the separation between the child means $(\bar{y}_A - \bar{y}_B)^2$, which by variance decomposition strictly increases information gain.
Therefore, an algorithm only needs to evaluate the $K-1$ adjacent splits along the sorted order!
Complexity: Sorting costs $\mathcal{O}(K \log K)$, and evaluating $K-1$ splits costs $\mathcal{O}(K)$. Total time collapses from $\mathcal{O}(2^K)$ to $\mathcal{O}(K \log K)$!

Tier 4: Conceptual Trap MCQs & Assertion-Reasoning

Problem 2.4.7 Medium Google

QUESTION: Which of the following transformations applied to feature column $X_1$ will alter the split decisions, predictions, or structure of a CART Decision Tree?

  1. Multiplying $X_1$ by a positive constant $c = 1000.0$.
  2. Adding a constant bias $b = -500.0$ to $X_1$.
  3. Applying any strictly monotonic transformation, such as $X_1' = \ln(X_1)$ (for $X_1 > 0$).
  4. Applying a non-monotonic quadratic transformation $X_1' = (X_1 - \mu)^2$.
✓ Complete Conceptual Analysis & Explanation

Correct Option: D

Exhaustive Analysis of All Options:

  • Option D WILL alter the tree: A quadratic transformation is not monotonic (points with different original values map to the same squared distance). This scrambles the sort order of the data points, altering candidate split partitions.
  • Options A, B, and C will NOT alter the tree: Decision tree splitting rules depend strictly on the rank order of feature values, never their absolute numerical scale. For any strictly monotonic function $g(x)$, $x_i \le \theta \iff g(x_i) \le g(\theta)$. The partition of samples on the left and right remains identical. Decision trees are completely invariant to monotonic feature scaling (making standardization and normalization redundant).

Problem 2.4.8 Hard DeepMind

QUESTION: Consider the following Assertion (A) and Reason (R):

Assertion (A): Standard CART decision trees perform exceptionally poorly on simple linear classification problems where the true separating boundary is a diagonal hyperplane $x_1 + x_2 = 1$.

Reason (R): Decision tree splits are constrained to axis-aligned orthogonal cuts ($x_j \le \theta$), forcing the tree to approximate smooth diagonal boundaries through a jagged "staircase" pattern that requires exponential leaf growth $\mathcal{O}(2^d)$ to achieve high precision.

  1. Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
  2. Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
  3. (A) is true, but (R) is false.
  4. (A) is false, but (R) is true.
✓ Complete Conceptual Analysis & Explanation

Correct Option: A

Exhaustive Analysis of Assertion & Reason:

  • Assertion (A) is TRUE: While a single logistic regression hyperplane separates $x_1 + x_2 = 1$ with $100\%$ accuracy and only 2 parameters, a standard decision tree needs dozens of nested levels to approximate the diagonal boundary, leading to high out-of-sample error and overfitting.
  • Reason (R) is TRUE: CART tests only one single feature per node ($x_1 \le \theta$ or $x_2 \le \theta$). Approximating a $45^\circ$ diagonal requires alternating vertical and horizontal cuts in a staircase, creating fragmented leaves with few samples.
  • Furthermore, Reason (R) is the exact geometric and architectural reason for Assertion (A).

5. Production Code Lab 2.4: CART Decision Tree from First Principles

Below is an educational, production-style implementation of a binary CART Decision Tree classifier written in pure Python without scikit-learn.

Code Lab 2.4 — Recursive Binary CART Classifier

🔗 View in GitHub: part2_classical_ml/ch24_decision_trees/decision_tree_scratch.py

import numpy as np

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, feature=None, threshold=None, left=None, right=None, *, value=None):
        self.feature = feature
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.left = left
        self.right = right
        self.value = value

    @property
    def is_leaf(self):
        return self.value is not None

class DecisionTreeClassifierScratch:
    def __init__(self, max_depth=5, min_samples_split=2):
        self.max_depth = max_depth
        self.min_samples_split = min_samples_split
        self.root = None

    def _gini(self, y):
        counts = np.bincount(y)
        probs = counts / len(y)
        return 1.0 - np.sum(probs ** 2)

    def _best_split(self, X, y):
        best_gain = -1.0
        split_feat, split_thresh = None, None
        parent_gini = self._gini(y)

        n_samples, n_features = X.shape
        for feat in range(n_features):
            thresholds = np.unique(X[:, feat])
            for thresh in thresholds:
                left_mask = X[:, feat] <= thresh
                right_mask = ~left_mask

                if np.sum(left_mask) == 0 or np.sum(right_mask) == 0:
                    continue

                # Weighted Gini impurity
                n_l, n_r = np.sum(left_mask), np.sum(right_mask)
                gini_l = self._gini(y[left_mask])
                gini_r = self._gini(y[right_mask])
                weighted_gini = (n_l / n_samples) * gini_l + (n_r / n_samples) * gini_r
                gain = parent_gini - weighted_gini

                if gain > best_gain:
                    best_gain = gain
                    split_feat = feat
                    split_thresh = thresh

        return split_feat, split_thresh

    def _build_tree(self, X, y, depth=0):
        n_samples, n_features = X.shape
        n_labels = len(np.unique(y))

        # Stopping criteria: pure node, max depth, or min samples
        if depth >= self.max_depth or n_labels == 1 or n_samples < self.min_samples_split:
            leaf_value = np.bincount(y).argmax()
            return TreeNode(value=leaf_value)

        feat, thresh = self._best_split(X, y)
        if feat is None:
            return TreeNode(value=np.bincount(y).argmax())

        left_mask = X[:, feat] <= thresh
        right_mask = ~left_mask

        left_child = self._build_tree(X[left_mask], y[left_mask], depth + 1)
        right_child = self._build_tree(X[right_mask], y[right_mask], depth + 1)
        return TreeNode(feature=feat, threshold=thresh, left=left_child, right=right_child)

    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.root = self._build_tree(X, y)

    def _predict_sample(self, x, node):
        if node.is_leaf:
            return node.value
        if x[node.feature] <= node.threshold:
            return self._predict_sample(x, node.left)
        return self._predict_sample(x, node.right)

    def predict(self, X):
        return np.array([self._predict_sample(x, self.root) for x in X])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
    data = load_iris()
    X, y = data.data, data.target
    clf = DecisionTreeClassifierScratch(max_depth=3)
    clf.fit(X, y)
    preds = clf.predict(X)
    print(f"CART Training Accuracy: {np.mean(preds == y) * 100:.2f}%")

Chapter 2.5

Ensemble Methods: Random Forests & Bagging

Variance Reduction, The 63.2% Bootstrap Theorem, Out-of-Bag Error & Feature Importance ✦

"None of us is as smart as all of us."

— Ken Blanchard

Foundation • Core Pillar

1. The Mathematics of Ensemble Variance Reduction

Individual decision trees are high-variance, low-bias estimators: a minor perturbation to the training dataset completely alters the split thresholds throughout the entire tree hierarchy. How can we eliminate this structural instability without sacrificing non-linear capacity?

The Variance of Averaged Correlated Estimators

Suppose we train $B$ separate estimators $\hat{f}_1, \hat{f}_2, \dots, \hat{f}_B$, each with identical variance $\text{Var}(\hat{f}_i) = \sigma^2$ and positive pairwise correlation $\text{Corr}(\hat{f}_i, \hat{f}_j) = \rho \in [0, 1]$ for all $i \neq j$. Consider the ensemble average estimator $\bar{f} = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^B \hat{f}_i$. The total variance of the ensemble is:

$$\text{Var}(\bar{f}) = \text{Var}\left( \frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^B \hat{f}_i \right) = \frac{1}{B^2} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^B \text{Var}(\hat{f}_i) + \sum_{i=1}^B \sum_{j \neq i}^B \text{Cov}(\hat{f}_i, \hat{f}_j) \right]$$

Substitute $\text{Var}(\hat{f}_i) = \sigma^2$ and $\text{Cov}(\hat{f}_i, \hat{f}_j) = \rho \sigma^2$ across all $B(B-1)$ off-diagonal pairs:

$$\text{Var}(\bar{f}) = \frac{1}{B^2} \left[ B \sigma^2 + B(B - 1) \rho \sigma^2 \right] = \frac{\sigma^2}{B} + \frac{B - 1}{B} \rho \sigma^2$$ $$\text{Var}(\bar{f}) = \rho \sigma^2 + \frac{1 - \rho}{B} \sigma^2$$

The Fundamental Law of Ensembles:

  • As the number of trees grows large ($B \to \infty$), the second term vanishes: $\lim_{B \to \infty} \frac{1 - \rho}{B} \sigma^2 = 0$.
  • The remaining variance is strictly bounded from below by the pairwise correlation: $\lim_{B \to \infty} \text{Var}(\bar{f}) = \mathbf{\rho \sigma^2}$.
Critical Engineering Implication: If all trees make identical predictions ($\rho = 1$), averaging 10,000 trees achieves zero variance reduction! To minimize error, an ensemble algorithm must actively decorrelate the base learners (minimize $\rho$) while keeping individual model strength high!

2. Bootstrap Aggregation (Bagging) & The 63.2% Theorem

Bootstrap Aggregation (Bagging) decorrelates trees by training each tree on an independently drawn bootstrap sample: drawing $N$ samples from dataset $\mathcal{D}$ of size $N$ with replacement.

📐 The 63.2% Bootstrap Theorem Dissected

When sampling $N$ items with replacement from a dataset of size $N$, what is the probability that any specific sample $i$ is NEVER selected?

  1. On any individual random draw, the probability of NOT selecting sample $i$ is: $$P(\text{Not picked in 1 draw}) = 1 - \frac{1}{N}$$
  2. Since all $N$ draws are mutually independent, the probability of NOT being picked in all $N$ draws is: $$P(\text{Excluded from bootstrap}) = \left( 1 - \frac{1}{N} \right)^N$$
  3. Taking the calculus limit as dataset size $N \to \infty$ (using the definition of the mathematical constant $e$): $$\lim_{N \to \infty} \left( 1 - \frac{1}{N} \right)^N = e^{-1} = \frac{1}{e} \approx 0.367879 = \mathbf{36.8\%}$$

Conversely, the probability that sample $i$ appears at least once in the bootstrap sample is $1 - e^{-1} \approx \mathbf{63.2\%}$!

Out-of-Bag (OOB) Validation Error

Because each tree leaves out approximately $36.8\%$ of the dataset, these unselected samples are called Out-of-Bag (OOB) samples. For every training sample $\mathbf{x}_i$, we can evaluate its prediction using only the subset of trees that never saw $\mathbf{x}_i$ during training:

$$\hat{y}_i^{\text{OOB}} = \arg\max_k \sum_{b: \mathbf{x}_i \notin \mathcal{D}_b} \mathbb{I}(\hat{f}_b(\mathbf{x}_i) = k)$$

This provides an unbiased, built-in cross-validation score without setting aside an explicit test set or executing computationally expensive $K$-Fold cross-validation.

3. Random Forests & Dual Feature Importance Metrics

Bagging alone is insufficient when one feature is overwhelmingly strong (e.g. account balance in fraud detection): every single bootstrap tree will pick that same dominant feature at the root node, causing high tree correlation $\rho$.

Random Forests (Breiman, 2001) introduce a second layer of randomization: at every candidate split, the tree is forbidden from searching across all $d$ features. Instead, it randomly selects a small subset of $m$ features:

$$m = \lfloor \sqrt{d} \rfloor \quad (\text{Classification}), \qquad m = \lfloor d / 3 \rfloor \quad (\text{Regression})$$

By forcing trees to split on suboptimal surrogate features, Random Forests drastically reduce pairwise tree correlation $\rho$, driving ensemble variance down to near zero.

Mean Decrease in Impurity (MDI) vs. Permutation Feature Importance (MDA)

Property Mean Decrease in Impurity (MDI / Gini Importance) Mean Decrease in Accuracy (MDA / Permutation Importance)
Mechanism Sums all Gini impurity reductions $\Delta I$ across all nodes where feature $j$ splits, weighted by sample proportion. Permutes (shuffles) values of feature $j$ on OOB samples and measures the drop in prediction accuracy.
Computational Cost $\mathcal{O}(1)$ (computed for free during tree training). $\mathcal{O}(B \cdot N)$ (requires evaluating all trees on shuffled OOB data).
Critical Trap Severe Cardinality Bias: Heavily inflates numerical features with many unique values (e.g. IDs or timestamps) even if completely uninformative! Unbiased: True gold standard. Shuffling a noise feature has zero impact on OOB accuracy regardless of cardinality.
